newsitem.title: FRANCE: Extreme-right victory in France alarms Europe.
newsitem.headline: Extreme-right victory in France alarms Europe.

text.p: European media sounded alarm bells on Tuesday at the growth of xenophobia and racism in France after the extreme-right National Front captured a fourth southern town in a local election.
Belgium's hard-right Flemish nationalist Vlaams Blok hailed Sunday's triumph of an anti-immigration French soulmate in the town of Vitrolles, north of Marseille, as an inspiration.
"What is possible in Vitrolles, Toulon, Marignane and Organe must be possible as well in Antwerp, Brussels and other Flemish cities," Vlaams Blok politician Filip Dewinter said.

European newspapers said the rise of Jean-Marie Le Pen's party, which advocates expelling three million immigrants and reserving jobs, homes and social services for French natives was a danger signal that should prompt soul-searching in France.
The victory of Catherine Megret, wife of the party's number two, was cheered by a crowd chanting "France for the French".
"A large part of the French right --and in quite a few cases of the left -- should look into their own hearts to see how much xenophobia shelters there," Spain's left-of-centre El Pais said.
Italian newspapers agreed, blaming France's major parties for allowing Jean-Marie Le Pen to chalk up yet another victory.
"No party has responded to Le Pen's racism with adequate policies," Rome's La Repubblica said in an editorial.

"The extreme right has turned the urban slums into electoral tanks in which most of the country's most serious problems are concentrated: high unemployment, crime and a large immigrant presence," it said.
In Dublin, the Irish Times said there should be no mistaking the political import of the election, which some French politicians had played down as a special local situation.

"The National Front...is an expressly racist organisation," it said. The party had thrived on mounting unemployment and the relative failure of successive governments to absorb the flow of immigrants from North Africa over the last 30 years.
The Front's rise was reinforced by a widespread belief that the French political class was riddled with corruption, it said.
In Britain, The Times expressed concern that the Front was gradually achieving its aim of respectability.

"The Front once seemed extreme; today it no longer worries voters. Like the far right Freedom party of Jorg Haider in Austria, the French Front's candidates are younger, smarter and more photogenic," the conservative daily said.
Russia's liberal daily Sevodnya criticised French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette for saying the choice between voting Socialist or National Front was like "choosing between plague and cholera".

"Politicians themselves agree that Le Pen asks the real questions, even if he gives monstrous answers. But apart from him, no one wants to answer these questions, above all because no one can," the Moscow newspaper said.

The mayor of the German town of Moerfelden-Walldorf, near Frankfurt, which is twinned with Vitrolles, said he planned to step up contact with its French sister town even though it would now be run by "fascists".

"(Megret) got more than 52 percent of the vote. All these people are not fascists," Social Democrat Bernhard Brehl told Reuters. "We have had friendly relations for years. We cannot turn our back on them and say it is all finished."
The conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said the result was no surprise in a region which has become fertile ground for the National Front.

"The question is how the conservative parties react to this," the paper said. While mainstream right leaders opposed against any kind of pandering to the National Front, others such as former interior minister Charles Pasqua favoured "taking over" Le Pen's favourite topics, it said.
